subject: PriTech streaming + TTFT decision & pilot plan

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>

Cc: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-09-12T15:22:00-07:00
Subject: Follow-up: TTFT/streaming items from today's discovery

Alex — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and a proposed next step so we keep momentum: 

Summary of requirements you mentioned
- UX: users must see first token within ~150ms p95 on short answers (FAQ-style, ~40-120 token responses). For longer generative outputs, first token p95 can be relaxed to ~300ms.
- Throughput/concurrency: peak concurrency expected 120-180 concurrent sessions during business hours; average concurrency ~40. Sustained throughput target ~6k requests/hour.
- Streaming: native streaming is required (progressive display) — you prefer SSE for browser clients but are open to WebSocket if SSE doesn't meet chunk/latency needs.
- Chunk cadence: you called out wanting small frequent chunks so users see output steadily rather than in large jumps — target cadence ~80–200ms between visible updates for short answers.

Immediate ask / next steps
1) We'll propose a pilot config and measurement plan (load profile + synthetic test corpus). Expect a proposed pilot doc attached.
2) Please confirm whether you require end-to-end encryption for streaming connections or if standard TLS is sufficient — this affects deployment topology for Private vs Hosted.
3) We'll schedule a 90-minute pilot run with engineering next Wed or Thu — which day works for your team?

Attached: redwood-ttft-proposal.pdf (pilot config + SLOs), sse-vs-ws-latency-chart.png.

If that summary looks good I'll ask our infra lead (Irene) to propose an initial pilot config and Monica to pull contract/PO guidance.

Thanks,
Rishi
Rishi Malhotra | Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Follow-up: TTFT/streaming items from today's discovery

Thanks Rishi — helpful summary. A few clarifications from our side: 

- The 150ms p95 for first token on short answers is our aspirational target. If you can hit <=150ms p95 with SSE in the hosted environment we can proceed. If SSE shows higher variance we may accept WebSocket for lower variance, but browser clients prefer the simplicity of SSE.
- For chunk cadence: examples would be great. We want visible character-level updates for short responses (so chunks shouldn't be >150 tokens for short answers). Our product folks mentioned a visible-update cadence of roughly 100ms feels smooth.
- Security: TLS is sufficient for now; we may request private deployment for regulated customer demos later — we'll flag that if/when the need arises.

We can do the pilot next Thursday (2026-09-17) in the morning PST. Please send the measurement harness and the test corpus. Also please send a simple one-page pilot SOW and estimated costs so we can route to procurement.

On the attachments: I saw the chart — can you confirm what workload assumptions produced the SSE vs WS latency lines? Was that single-tenant dedicated GPUs or multi-tenant hosted?

—Alex
Alex Chen | Head of Product | PriTech Solutions
From: Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.ai>

Subject: Pilot config + measurement notes (SSE vs WS)

Hi Alex — quick technical note on the chart and a recommended pilot config.

About the chart: the SSE vs WS lines in sse-vs-ws-latency-chart.png came from a controlled pilot we ran on a dedicated 4xA100 pool with the following: model = 13B open-arch (fp16 quantized path we use in Hosted), sequence profile = 40–200 tokens, concurrency sweep = 50–400, and synthetic prompt mix skewed to short answers (avg 70 tokens). SSE ordering in that run used our small-chunk flush strategy (chunks ~64 tokens, flush on new token availability), and WebSocket runs used identical runtime but a different client-side buffer strategy — we observed slightly lower median jitter with WebSocket at high concurrency (300+), primarily due to TCP windowing and fewer intermediary proxies in the test harness. 

Recommended pilot config for PriTech (to reproduce your target):
- Environment: Hosted Redwood (we can run same config in Dedicated if you want isolation)
- Model: curated 13B variant (quantized) — good balance for cost/latency on short responses
- Serving pool: 4xA100 equivalent; autoscale buffer + 1 spare node for fallback
- Concurrency target for tests: ramp to 200 concurrent sessions (sustained 2 min windows, peak to 180–220 for 30s bursts)
- Requests: 6k/hr sustained as Rishi noted; test suite will include a 10-minute steady-state run and a 5-minute burst run
- Streaming settings: SSE preferred; chunking strategy = small prefix chunks (<=64 tokens) + immediate flush; target visible-update cadence ~= 80–120ms on median under expected load. We will instrument to measure visible-update percentiles (p50/p95/p99) and the Time-To-First-Token p50/p95/p99.

Measurement harness and test corpus: I've uploaded the harness and sample corpus to the Drive link Rishi included. The harness uses our continuous-batching client that emulates browser SSE consumption (it opens an SSE stream and records timestamps for first byte and subsequent chunk arrivals). The key metrics we'll capture: TTFT p50/p95/p99, chunk cadence p50/p95, throughput (req/s), and token cost.

On the decision between SSE and WS: for the pilot we recommend starting with SSE using the small-chunk flush settings above. If you see high p95 jitter in SSE during burst scenarios we'll test the same runtime over WebSocket and compare. In our experience, WebSocket reduces network-layer jitter slightly in some cloud networking topologies, but SSE is simplest to integrate on modern browsers.

Next steps I'll take this week:
- Finalize the pilot runbook (I'll send a one-page SOW version)
- Prepare Grafana dashboards for the run and short-term access for your engops team

Rishi / Monica: can you confirm procurement path so Alex has PO guidance?

Thanks,
Irene
